reason: The text, from Exodus 16, emphasizes that what distinguishes the Hebrew people and sustains their identity is their obedience to Yahweh's commandments and laws. God explicitly tests them ('לְמַעַן אֲנַסֶּנּוּ הֲיֵלֵךְ בְּתוֹרָתִי' - 'to test whether you will walk in my law') and later expresses frustration at their failure to keep His commandments ('עַד־ אָנָה מֵאַנְתֶּם לִשְׁמֹר מִצְוֺתַי וְתוֹרֹתָֽי' - 'how long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws'). The Sabbath observance is presented as a divine institution that defines their covenant relationship with Yahweh. While the text emphasizes law-keeping and covenant obedience rather than ritual worship per se, these elements constitute the 'worship' of Yahweh in the sense of devoted allegiance and religious practice. The passage demonstrates that what makes the Hebrews a distinct people is precisely their binding relationship with Yahweh expressed through obedience to His laws.
